Output and loss, for programmers

The output layer as a choice of distribution (identity, sigmoid, softmax), the softmax with its Jacobian, its invariance and its temperature, the regression losses (MSE, MAE, Huber) and the classification losses (binary and categorical cross-entropy from logits), why the canonical pair gives the gradient and squared error on a sigmoid does not, each loss as a negative log-likelihood, several heads with weights, and class weights with costs in dollars. With a from-scratch module checked against PyTorch, scikit-learn and finite differences, and a worked example by hand.

Summary

  • The output sets the range of the prediction: identity for quantities, sigmoid for a probability, softmax for mutually exclusive classes. Each one has its natural loss, the negative log-likelihood of a Gaussian, a Bernoulli or a categorical.
  • : subtract before exponentiating. With in float64 (89 in float32) the naive version gives nan.
  • With the canonical pair, . With squared error after a sigmoid, the factor appears and kills the gradient exactly when the network is confident and wrong.
  • MSE picks the conditional mean and is sensitive to outliers; MAE, the median; Huber is quadratic up to and linear beyond.
  • With several heads, : units matter. A class weight in the BCE is equivalent to shifting the logit by , that is, to alerting from ; with it is the minimum-cost decision.
hidden layers→ logits z→ g: identity, σ, softmax→ loss = −log p(y)→ ∂L/∂z = p − y→ landscape over θ

§1 · The output

The last layer chooses a distribution

The hidden layers of the multilayer network produce a representation . The output layer is affine, (the logits), followed by a function that maps to the space of what is being predicted. In this topic's network, a shared body and three heads:

with the fuel use in L/100 km, the probability of a breakdown in 30 days and the split across urban, regional and highway ( is the simplex: nonnegative vectors that add up to 1). The table in topic 2, §6 already summarized the pairs; here, with what you write in PyTorch:

PredictedgRangeLoss∂ℓ/∂zPyTorch (takes z)
quantity (L/100 km)identityMSELoss, HuberLoss
yes/no (breakdown)sigmoidBCEBCEWithLogitsLoss
1 of K (trip type)softmaxCECrossEntropyLoss
several labels at oncesigmoid per outputBCE per outputBCEWithLogitsLoss

Two classic mistakes: putting nn.Softmax before CrossEntropyLoss (which already applies log_softmax; the model learns, but with shrunken gradients) and nn.Sigmoid + BCELoss instead of BCEWithLogitsLoss (it loses the stable form and clips at ). The output activation is applied only when predicting.

§2 · Softmax

Exponentiate and normalize, with its Jacobian

Properties used every day:

  • Shift invariance. : the factor cancels out. That is why and logits have degrees of freedom. With and , : the sigmoid is the two-class softmax.
  • Stability. It is computed with : , the denominator is at least 1 and there is no overflow and no 0/0 division. Same for ; topic 15, §5 develops it together with the clipping in log_loss.
  • Temperature. Dividing by keeps the order (the ) and changes the confidence: tends to the one-hot of the maximum, to the uniform. It is used for sampling in language models, for distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) and for post-hoc recalibration (Guo et al., 2017).

desborde.py · the toy's trip, shifts, temperature and overflow · actual output

"""Naive vs stable softmax: overflow, shift invariance and temperature."""
import warnings
import numpy as np
from perdidas import softmax, logsumexp

warnings.simplefilter("always")

def softmax_ingenuo(z):
    e = np.exp(z); return e / e.sum()

z = np.array([0.4, 1.6, 0.9])                       # urban, regional, highway (the toy's trip)
print("logits", z, "→ softmax", softmax(z).round(4))
print("  + 100 to all three:", softmax(z + 100).round(4), " (adding the same changes nothing)")
for T in (0.5, 1, 2, 5):
    print(f"  temperature T = {T}: {softmax(z, T).round(4)}  (the order is kept)")
for desplaz in (700, 710, 1000):
    with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
        r = softmax_ingenuo(z + desplaz)
    print(f"naive with z + {desplaz}: {r}  warnings {[x.category.__name__ for x in w]}")
print("stable with z + 1000:", softmax(z + 1000).round(4))
print("naive with z − 800:", end=" ")
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    print(softmax_ingenuo(z - 800), [x.category.__name__ for x in w])
z32 = (z + 89).astype(np.float32)
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    print("float32 with z + 89:", softmax_ingenuo(z32), [x.category.__name__ for x in w])
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as w:
    ing = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(z + 1000)))
print(f"logsumexp(z + 1000) = {logsumexp(z + 1000):.4f}   naive: {ing}  warnings {[x.category.__name__ for x in w]}")
# logits [0.4 1.6 0.9] → softmax [0.1675 0.5562 0.2762]
#   + 100 to all three: [0.1675 0.5562 0.2762]  (adding the same changes nothing)
#   temperature T = 0.5: [0.0678 0.7478 0.1844]  (the order is kept)
#   temperature T = 1: [0.1675 0.5562 0.2762]  (the order is kept)
#   temperature T = 2: [0.2435 0.4438 0.3127]  (the order is kept)
#   temperature T = 5: [0.2962 0.3765 0.3273]  (the order is kept)
# naive with z + 700: [0.16753679 0.55624174 0.27622147]  warnings []
# naive with z + 710: [nan nan nan]  warnings ['RuntimeWarning', 'RuntimeWarning']
# naive with z + 1000: [nan nan nan]  warnings ['RuntimeWarning', 'RuntimeWarning']
# stable with z + 1000: [0.1675 0.5562 0.2762]
# naive with z − 800: [nan nan nan] ['RuntimeWarning']
# float32 with z + 89: [nan nan nan] ['RuntimeWarning', 'RuntimeWarning']
# logsumexp(z + 1000) = 1002.1866   naive: inf  warnings ['RuntimeWarning']

is the largest representable exponential in float64; with numerator and denominator are inf and inf/inf gives nan. In float32 the limit is , and logits of 90 show up in unnormalized networks. Downward the failure is symmetric: with everything rounds to 0 and you get 0/0. The version that subtracts the maximum gives the same three percentages in every case.

§3 · Regression

MSE, MAE and Huber: which statistic each one estimates

With and the mean over the batch:

If the network could output any function, the population MSE is minimized by the conditional mean and the MAE by the conditional median. For a constant over a sample, that is the mean and the median. The MSE gradient grows with the error, so an outlier with error pulls with force ; the MAE and Huber gradients are bounded (by 1 and by ). Huber (1964) proposed it as a robust location estimator; in PyTorch, smooth_l1_loss with parameter is .

atipico.py · 10 trips on one route, the tenth with the tank sensor misread · actual output

"""The best single number for 10 trips on one route according to the loss: MSE → mean, MAE → median,
Huber → something in between. The tenth trip was misread by the sensor (95 L/100 km)."""
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize_scalar
from datos import RUTA, ATIPICO
from perdidas import mse, mae, huber

buenos = np.array(RUTA)
for nombre, y in (("without outlier", buenos), ("with outlier", np.r_[buenos, ATIPICO])):
    mejor = {"MSE": y.mean(), "MAE": np.median(y),
             "Huber δ=2": minimize_scalar(lambda c: huber(c, y, 2.0), bounds=(20, 100), method="bounded", options={"xatol": 1e-9}).x}
    print(f"{nombre:15s} " + "   ".join(f"{k}: {v:6.2f}" for k, v in mejor.items()))
ref = buenos.mean()
y = np.r_[buenos, ATIPICO]
e = ATIPICO - ref
print(f"outlier error vs {ref:.2f}: {e:.1f} L/100 km → penalty MSE {e**2:.0f}, MAE {abs(e):.1f}, "
      f"Huber {2 * (abs(e) - 1):.1f}")
print(f"outlier's share of the total loss: MSE {e**2 / (len(y) * mse(ref, y)):.1%}"
      f"  MAE {abs(e) / (len(y) * mae(ref, y)):.1%}")
# without outlier MSE:  33.10   MAE:  33.10   Huber δ=2:  33.11
# with outlier    MSE:  39.29   MAE:  33.35   Huber δ=2:  33.43
# outlier error vs 33.10: 61.9 L/100 km → penalty MSE 3832, MAE 61.9, Huber 121.8
# outlier's share of the total loss: MSE 99.2%  MAE 81.8%

A single 95 L/100 km trip takes 99.2% of the sum of squares around 33.10 and shifts the mean by 6.19 L; the median moves 0.25 and Huber 0.32. The MAE has its costs: its gradient does not vanish near the optimum (it only changes sign), which forces a lower learning rate, and at it is not differentiable (libraries take ). Huber combines the best of both with a on the order of the normal noise in the data: here, 2 L/100 km.

§4 · Classification

Cross-entropy from the logits and the gradient p − y

Topic 15 derives cross-entropy from information theory and studies it as a proper scoring rule. What matters here is how it is written and differentiated with respect to the logits. For the binary case, with and :

For classes, with the true class and its one-hot:

The same computation by the chain rule (topic 16): and, by the Jacobian in §2,

The of the Jacobian cancels the of the logarithm: that is why the gradient has no factor that vanishes. It is bounded () even though the loss is not: when .

A sigmoid with BCE is logistic regression and a softmax with CE, multinomial logistic regression: the network only changes where comes from.

§5 · Saturation

Why not squared error on a probability

With ,

The factor from topic 2 vanishes in the tails: if and , the gradient is versus with cross-entropy. Moreover, is not convex in , while the BCE of logistic regression is: it has a single valley. Golik, Doetsch and Ney (2013) compare them in speech recognition networks: squared error trains worse from random initializations and is useful, at most, for fine-tuning.

saturacion.py · gradients for y = 1 and a neuron that starts backwards · actual output

"""Why not squared error on probabilities: the push on z for a truck that DID break down,
and a sigmoid neuron trained from a bad start with each loss (PyTorch, autograd)."""
import numpy as np
import torch
from datos import camiones
from perdidas import sigmoide

print(" z     p        CE=−log p   CE push = p−1      MSE=(p−1)²   MSE push = 2(p−1)p(1−p)")
for z in (-6, -4, -2, 0, 2):
    p = sigmoide(z)
    print(f"{z:3d}  {p:.4f}   {-np.log(p):8.3f}     {p - 1:+.4f}          {(p - 1) ** 2:.4f}       {2 * (p - 1) * p * (1 - p):+.5f}")

x, y = camiones(40, seed=4)                       # 40 trucks: thousands of km since inspection and breakdown yes/no
u = torch.tensor((x - 30) / 30); t = torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float64)
print(f"\n40 trucks, {int(y.sum())} breakdowns. Neuron p = σ(b + w·u), u = (km − 30,000)/30,000.")
print("Starts backwards (w = −6: “more km, fewer breakdowns”), gradient descent with step 0.5:")
for nombre in ("cross-entropy", "squared error on p"):
    w = torch.tensor(-6.0, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
    b = torch.tensor(-2.5, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
    fila = []
    for paso in range(1, 2001):
        z = b + w * u
        L = torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(z, t) if nombre.startswith("cross") \
            else torch.mean((torch.sigmoid(z) - t) ** 2)
        w.grad = b.grad = None; L.backward()
        if paso == 1: g0 = w.grad.item()
        with torch.no_grad(): w -= 0.5 * w.grad; b -= 0.5 * b.grad
        if paso in (10, 100, 2000): fila.append(f"step {paso}: w = {w.item():+.2f}")
    print(f"  {nombre:25s} initial gradient in w {g0:+.4f}   " + "   ".join(fila))
#  z     p        CE=−log p   CE push = p−1      MSE=(p−1)²   MSE push = 2(p−1)p(1−p)
#  -6  0.0025      6.002     -0.9975          0.9951       -0.00492
#  -4  0.0180      4.018     -0.9820          0.9644       -0.03469
#  -2  0.1192      2.127     -0.8808          0.7758       -0.18496
#   0  0.5000      0.693     -0.5000          0.2500       -0.25000
#   2  0.8808      0.127     -0.1192          0.0142       -0.02503
# 
# 40 trucks, 7 breakdowns. Neuron p = σ(b + w·u), u = (km − 30,000)/30,000.
# Starts backwards (w = −6: “more km, fewer breakdowns”), gradient descent with step 0.5:
#   cross-entropy             initial gradient in w -0.2057   step 10: w = -5.00   step 100: w = +0.64   step 2000: w = +2.46
#   squared error on p        initial gradient in w -0.0288   step 10: w = -5.85   step 100: w = -4.84   step 2000: w = -3.53

From (more kilometers, fewer breakdowns), the BCE makes in under 100 steps and after 2,000 reaches 2.46, the optimum (scikit-learn gives 2.45 with a free bias). With squared error, the initial gradient is 7 times smaller and after 2,000 steps is still at −3.53: the neuron still says the opposite of what happens. The widget draws both full landscapes over .

The 40 trucks of the example, with and . The color is the average loss on a log scale, normalized separately for each loss. The BCE is a single valley with walls that never flatten out; squared error on has plateaus in the corners (with very negative or very negative , every prediction saturates) that descent barely gets out of. This landscape is the one topic 5, backpropagation, learns to traverse in networks with thousands of weights, and the one gradient descent walks down.

§6 · Likelihood

Each loss is a negative log-likelihood

If the network outputs the parameters of a distribution , the maximum likelihood loss (topic 14) is . Depending on the distribution:

With or fixed, the constant terms do not change the optimum: minimizing the MSE means assuming Gaussian noise with constant variance, and the MAE, Laplace noise. The MSE is no longer an arbitrary choice: it follows from a noise model, and if that model is bad (heavy tails, failing sensors) so is the loss. If the network also predicts , the full Gaussian is GaussianNLLLoss and it learns the uncertainty of each trip.

verosimilitud.py · checked with scipy.stats and torch.distributions · actual output

"""Each loss is a mean negative log-likelihood: Gaussian → MSE, Laplace → MAE,
Bernoulli → BCE, categorical → CE. Checked with scipy.stats and torch.distributions."""
import numpy as np
import torch
from scipy import stats
import perdidas as P

rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
n = 1000
yhat = rng.uniform(25, 45, n)                       # fuel use the network predicts (L/100 km)
y = yhat + rng.normal(0, 1.5, n)                    # what was measured: prediction + Gaussian noise with σ = 1.5
s = 1.5
nll = -np.mean(stats.norm.logpdf(y, yhat, s))
print(f"Gaussian σ = {s}: mean −log-likelihood {nll:.6f}")
print(f"   MSE/(2σ²) + ½·log(2πσ²)              {P.mse(yhat, y) / (2 * s**2) + 0.5 * np.log(2 * np.pi * s**2):.6f}")
print(f"   torch GaussianNLLLoss(full=True)       "
      f"{torch.nn.GaussianNLLLoss(full=True)(torch.tensor(yhat), torch.tensor(y), torch.full((n,), s**2)).item():.6f}")
print(f"   σ² that maximizes the likelihood = MSE = {P.mse(yhat, y):.4f}  (σ = {np.sqrt(P.mse(yhat, y)):.3f})")
bL = 1.2
print(f"Laplace b = {bL}: −log-likelihood {-np.mean(stats.laplace.logpdf(y, yhat, bL)):.6f}"
      f" = MAE/b + log(2b) = {P.mae(yhat, y) / bL + np.log(2 * bL):.6f}")
z = rng.normal(-1.5, 2, n); yb = (rng.random(n) < P.sigmoide(z)).astype(int)
print(f"Bernoulli: −log-likelihood {-np.mean(stats.bernoulli.logpmf(yb, P.sigmoide(z))):.6f}"
      f" = BCE from logits {P.bce_logits(z, yb):.6f}")
Z = rng.normal(0, 2, (n, 3)); c = rng.integers(0, 3, n)
lp = torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=torch.tensor(Z)).log_prob(torch.tensor(c)).numpy()
print(f"categorical: −log-likelihood {-lp.mean():.6f} = CE from logits {P.ce_logits(Z, c):.6f}")
# Gaussian σ = 1.5: mean −log-likelihood 1.817565
#    MSE/(2σ²) + ½·log(2πσ²)              1.817565
#    torch GaussianNLLLoss(full=True)       1.817565
#    σ² that maximizes the likelihood = MSE = 2.2192  (σ = 1.490)
# Laplace b = 1.2: −log-likelihood 1.875131 = MAE/b + log(2b) = 1.875131
# Bernoulli: −log-likelihood 0.426879 = BCE from logits 0.426879
# categorical: −log-likelihood 2.043769 = CE from logits 2.043769

§7 · Weights

Several heads, class weights and dollars

Several heads. The total loss is , and the gradients of all of them add up in the shared body. The fuel-use MSE is measured in (L/100 km)² and the cross-entropy in nats: with , the head with big numbers dominates. The usual fix is to standardize the regression target (divide by its standard deviation, like the scaling in D7) and tune on validation. Kendall, Gal and Cipolla (2018) learn as variances of a Gaussian likelihood, consistent with §6.

Class weights. With a weight on the positives (pos_weight in PyTorch, class_weight in scikit-learn):

The pointwise minimizer of the weighted loss is the true log-odds plus . Training with weight and cutting at 0.5 is equivalent to training without weights and cutting at . The minimum expected cost decision alerts when , that is, when (Elkan, 2001). With a $4,000 roadside breakdown and a $300 unnecessary inspection, and the threshold is 300/4,300 = 0.0698. The alternative without retraining is to move the threshold: topic D6 compares both and resampling.

pesos.py · 2,000 training trucks and 2,000 test trucks · actual output

"""Class weights in binary cross-entropy: weighting each breakdown w times is the same as lowering the
alert threshold to 1/(1 + w). With w = cost of a breakdown / cost of an inspection, the cost is minimized."""
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from datos import camiones, COSTE_AVERIA, COSTE_REVISION

xe, ye = camiones(2000, seed=100)                  # training
xp, yp = camiones(2000, seed=101)                  # test: another 2,000 trucks
U = lambda x: ((x - 30) / 30)[:, None]
w = COSTE_AVERIA / COSTE_REVISION
print(f"breakdowns: {ye.mean():.1%} in training, {yp.mean():.1%} in test;  w = {COSTE_AVERIA}/{COSTE_REVISION} = {w:.2f}")
m1 = LogisticRegression(C=1e6).fit(U(xe), ye)
mw = LogisticRegression(C=1e6, class_weight={0: 1, 1: w}).fit(U(xe), ye)
print(f"no weights: b = {m1.intercept_[0]:.3f}, w_km = {m1.coef_[0, 0]:.3f}   weighted: b = {mw.intercept_[0]:.3f},"
      f" w_km = {mw.coef_[0, 0]:.3f}   difference in b {mw.intercept_[0] - m1.intercept_[0]:.3f} (log w = {np.log(w):.3f})")
usd = lambda c: f"${c:,.0f}"                       # dollars with a thousands comma
def coste(aviso):
    escapan, de_mas = np.sum((~aviso) & (yp == 1)), np.sum(aviso & (yp == 0))
    return escapan, de_mas, (escapan * COSTE_AVERIA + de_mas * COSTE_REVISION)       # $ on the 2,000 test trucks
p1, pw = m1.predict_proba(U(xp))[:, 1], mw.predict_proba(U(xp))[:, 1]
for nombre, aviso in [("no weights, threshold 0.5", p1 >= 0.5), (f"no weights, threshold 1/(1+w) = {1 / (1 + w):.4f}", p1 >= 1 / (1 + w)),
                      ("weighted, threshold 0.5", pw >= 0.5), ("alert everyone", np.ones_like(p1, bool)),
                      ("alert no one", np.zeros_like(p1, bool))]:
    e, d, c = coste(aviso)
    print(f"  {nombre:38s} missed breakdowns {e:4d}   extra inspections {d:5d}   cost {usd(c):>10s} on 2,000 trucks")
ws = np.arange(1, 61); cs = [coste(p1 >= 1 / (1 + k))[2] for k in ws]
print(f"sweep of w = 1…60 with threshold 1/(1+w): the lowest cost is {usd(min(cs))} with w = {ws[np.argmin(cs)]}")
print(f"km since inspection from which an alert is raised: threshold 0.5 → {30 + 30 * (-m1.intercept_[0] / m1.coef_[0, 0]):.1f} thousand;"
      f"  threshold {1 / (1 + w):.4f} → {30 + 30 * ((np.log(1 / w) - m1.intercept_[0]) / m1.coef_[0, 0]):.1f} thousand")
# breakdowns: 12.8% in training, 12.6% in test;  w = 4000/300 = 13.33
# no weights: b = -2.816, w_km = 2.945   weighted: b = -0.227, w_km = 2.937   difference in b 2.590 (log w = 2.590)
#   no weights, threshold 0.5              missed breakdowns  230   extra inspections    29   cost   $928,700 on 2,000 trucks
#   no weights, threshold 1/(1+w) = 0.0698 missed breakdowns   27   extra inspections   667   cost   $308,100 on 2,000 trucks
#   weighted, threshold 0.5                missed breakdowns   27   extra inspections   667   cost   $308,100 on 2,000 trucks
#   alert everyone                         missed breakdowns    0   extra inspections  1748   cost   $524,400 on 2,000 trucks
#   alert no one                           missed breakdowns  252   extra inspections     0   cost $1,008,000 on 2,000 trucks
# sweep of w = 1…60 with threshold 1/(1+w): the lowest cost is $300,300 with w = 12
# km since inspection from which an alert is raised: threshold 0.5 → 58.7 thousand;  threshold 0.0698 → 32.3 thousand

The weighted bias shifts by 2.590, exactly , and the slope barely changes: the logistic model is well specified, so the equivalence is almost exact and the decisions match truck by truck. Without weights, 230 of 252 breakdowns slip through ($928,700); with , 27 breakdowns and 667 extra inspections ($308,100). The sweep puts the minimum at ($300,300); the theoretical costs 2.6% more, sampling noise with only 252 breakdowns. Class weights change the probabilities: they are no longer calibrated. If you need honest probabilities (for budgeting, to combine them with other costs), train without weights and move the threshold.

§8 · From scratch

Outputs, losses and gradients in NumPy, checked

perdidas.py

"""Output activations, losses and their gradients, from scratch with NumPy (mean over the batch)."""
import numpy as np


def logsumexp(z, axis=-1):
    """log Σ e^z without overflow: the maximum is subtracted before exponentiating."""
    z = np.asarray(z, float)
    m = np.max(z, axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    return np.squeeze(m, axis) + np.log(np.sum(np.exp(z - m), axis=axis))


def softmax(z, T=1.0, axis=-1):
    """e^(z/T) normalized; subtracting the maximum does not change the result and avoids overflow."""
    z = np.asarray(z, float) / T
    e = np.exp(z - np.max(z, axis=axis, keepdims=True))
    return e / np.sum(e, axis=axis, keepdims=True)


def log_softmax(z, axis=-1):
    z = np.asarray(z, float)
    return z - np.expand_dims(logsumexp(z, axis), axis)


def sigmoide(z):
    z = np.asarray(z, float); e = np.exp(-np.abs(z))
    return np.where(z >= 0, 1 / (1 + e), e / (1 + e))


# ---------- regression: ŷ are numbers with no activation ----------
def mse(yhat, y):
    return np.mean((yhat - y) ** 2)

def d_mse(yhat, y):
    return 2 * (yhat - y) / np.size(y)

def mae(yhat, y):
    return np.mean(np.abs(yhat - y))

def d_mae(yhat, y):
    return np.sign(yhat - y) / np.size(y)

def huber(yhat, y, delta=1.0):
    """Quadratic if |e| ≤ δ, linear beyond: e²/2 or δ(|e| − δ/2)."""
    e = np.abs(yhat - y)
    return np.mean(np.where(e <= delta, 0.5 * e ** 2, delta * (e - 0.5 * delta)))

def d_huber(yhat, y, delta=1.0):
    return np.clip(yhat - y, -delta, delta) / np.size(y)


# ---------- classification: always from the logits ----------
def bce_logits(z, y, pos_weight=1.0):
    """−[w·y·log σ(z) + (1 − y)·log(1 − σ(z))] with log σ(z) = −softplus(−z), without forming σ(z)."""
    z = np.asarray(z, float)
    sp = lambda t: np.maximum(t, 0) + np.log1p(np.exp(-np.abs(t)))      # stable softplus
    return np.mean(pos_weight * y * sp(-z) + (1 - y) * sp(z))

def d_bce_logits(z, y, pos_weight=1.0):
    p = sigmoide(z)
    return (pos_weight * y * (p - 1) + (1 - y) * p) / np.size(y)        # with w = 1: (p − y)/n

def ce_logits(Z, c):
    """Mean cross-entropy: −log softmax(Z)[i, c_i] = logsumexp(Z_i) − Z_i[c_i]."""
    Z = np.asarray(Z, float); c = np.asarray(c)
    return np.mean(logsumexp(Z, axis=1) - Z[np.arange(len(c)), c])

def d_ce_logits(Z, c):
    P = softmax(Z, axis=1); P[np.arange(len(c)), c] -= 1                # p − y (y one-hot)
    return P / len(c)


def mse_sobre_p(z, y):
    """Squared error applied to the probability (what you should NOT do) and its gradient in z."""
    p = sigmoide(z)
    return np.mean((p - y) ** 2), 2 * (p - y) * p * (1 - p) / np.size(y)

check.py · against torch.nn.functional, PyTorch 2.15 autograd (CPU), sklearn.metrics.log_loss and central differences

"""Check of perdidas.py against torch.nn.functional, PyTorch autograd,
sklearn.metrics.log_loss and central differences (all in float64)."""
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from sklearn.metrics import log_loss
import perdidas as P

torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
n, K = 5000, 3
yhat, y = rng.normal(32, 6, n), rng.normal(32, 6, n)       # regression (L/100 km)
z, yb = rng.normal(0, 4, n), rng.integers(0, 2, n)          # binary logits and 0/1 labels
Z, c = rng.normal(0, 4, (n, K)), rng.integers(0, K, n)      # 3-class logits and the true class

def frente_a_torch(nombre, f, df, ref, x, *args):
    t = torch.tensor(x, requires_grad=True)
    v = ref(t, *[torch.tensor(a) for a in args]); v.backward()
    e_v = abs(f(x, *args) - v.item()); e_g = np.max(np.abs(df(x, *args) - t.grad.numpy()))
    print(f"  {nombre:28s} value {e_v:8.1e}   gradient {e_g:8.1e}")
    return max(e_v, e_g)

print(f"{n} examples · maximum absolute error vs PyTorch {torch.__version__}")
err = [frente_a_torch("MSE vs F.mse_loss", P.mse, P.d_mse, F.mse_loss, yhat, y),
       frente_a_torch("MAE vs F.l1_loss", P.mae, P.d_mae, F.l1_loss, yhat, y),
       frente_a_torch("Huber δ=2 vs F.huber_loss", lambda a, b: P.huber(a, b, 2.0),
                      lambda a, b: P.d_huber(a, b, 2.0), lambda a, b: F.huber_loss(a, b, delta=2.0), yhat, y),
       frente_a_torch("BCE vs F.bce_with_logits", P.bce_logits, P.d_bce_logits,
                      F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits, z, yb.astype(float)),
       frente_a_torch("BCE pos_weight=13.3", lambda a, b: P.bce_logits(a, b, 13.3),
                      lambda a, b: P.d_bce_logits(a, b, 13.3),
                      lambda a, b: F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(a, b, pos_weight=torch.tensor(13.3)),
                      z, yb.astype(float))]
t = torch.tensor(Z, requires_grad=True); v = F.cross_entropy(t, torch.tensor(c)); v.backward()
e = max(abs(P.ce_logits(Z, c) - v.item()), np.max(np.abs(P.d_ce_logits(Z, c) - t.grad.numpy())))
print(f"  {'CE vs F.cross_entropy':28s} value {abs(P.ce_logits(Z, c) - v.item()):8.1e}   gradient "
      f"{np.max(np.abs(P.d_ce_logits(Z, c) - t.grad.numpy())):8.1e}"); err.append(e)
for nombre, mio, ref in [("softmax vs F.softmax", P.softmax(Z, axis=1), F.softmax(torch.tensor(Z), 1)),
                         ("softmax T=2.5", P.softmax(Z, 2.5, axis=1), F.softmax(torch.tensor(Z) / 2.5, 1)),
                         ("log_softmax", P.log_softmax(Z, axis=1), F.log_softmax(torch.tensor(Z), 1)),
                         ("logsumexp", P.logsumexp(Z, axis=1), torch.logsumexp(torch.tensor(Z), 1))]:
    e = np.max(np.abs(mio - ref.numpy())); err.append(e); print(f"  {nombre:28s} value {e:8.1e}")
pb = P.sigmoide(z)
e1 = abs(P.bce_logits(z, yb) - log_loss(yb, pb)); e2 = abs(P.ce_logits(Z, c) - log_loss(c, P.softmax(Z, axis=1)))
print(f"  {'BCE vs sklearn log_loss':28s} value {e1:8.1e}\n  {'CE vs sklearn log_loss':28s} value {e2:8.1e}")
print(f"maximum of all the above: {max(err + [e1, e2]):.1e}")

h = 1e-6                                                    # central differences on a small batch
z8, y8 = z[:8], yb[:8]
num = np.array([(P.bce_logits(z8 + h * np.eye(8)[i], y8) - P.bce_logits(z8 - h * np.eye(8)[i], y8)) / (2 * h) for i in range(8)])
Z8, c8 = Z[:8], c[:8]
numc = np.array([[(P.ce_logits(Z8 + h * np.eye(24)[3 * i + k].reshape(8, 3), c8)
                   - P.ce_logits(Z8 - h * np.eye(24)[3 * i + k].reshape(8, 3), c8)) / (2 * h) for k in range(3)] for i in range(8)])
print(f"central differences (h = 1e-6): BCE {np.max(np.abs(num - P.d_bce_logits(z8, y8))):.1e}"
      f"   CE {np.max(np.abs(numc - P.d_ce_logits(Z8, c8))):.1e}")

With 5,000 examples and logits with standard deviation 4, everything matches PyTorch and scikit-learn to within , the rounding of adding 5,000 terms in float64. The gradients, compared with autograd on the mean loss, land at – because they are already divided by . Central differences with match to , the expected rounding error . The pos_weight case is the one in §7.

§9 · Checklist

Before training

  • Output according to the target type: identity, sigmoid (one or several labels) or softmax (one of K).
  • Losses take logits: BCEWithLogitsLoss and CrossEntropyLoss, with no sigmoid or softmax in front.
  • Your own implementations with max subtraction, logsumexp and stable softplus; checked against autograd in float64.
  • Regression target standardized; MAE or Huber if there are outliers that cannot be cleaned, with on the order of the noise.
  • With several heads, each loss on a comparable scale and chosen on validation; watch which head dominates the gradient.
  • Examples with huge losses, reviewed: they are often wrong labels.
  • Asymmetric costs: either class weights with , or threshold on calibrated probabilities; not both at once.

§10 · Worked example

A 180 km trip through the three heads

The three losses of the simple version's toy, computed by hand, added up and translated into liters and dollars.

The situation. A truck finishes a 180 km regional trip. Its actual fuel use was 33.0 L/100 km and, in the following 30 days, it had a breakdown. Before knowing that, the fleet's multitask network had given 31.2 L/100 km, a breakdown logit of −1.2 and type logits (0.4, 1.6, 0.9) for urban, regional and highway. How much does each head penalize, which one dominates the total loss, and what would it have taken to alert about the breakdown?

Example map

A single trip goes through the three heads of the network. In each one we turn the raw number into an answer, compute the loss by hand and the push the network would get. Then we add up the three losses, see what happens if the network had been confident and wrong, and translate the breakdown head into dollars.

  1. Fuel use: linear output and squared error.
  2. Breakdown: sigmoid and binary cross-entropy.
  3. Trip type: softmax and cross-entropy.
  4. The total loss and who dominates it.
  5. Confident and wrong.
  6. Dollars: the weight of a breakdown and the alert threshold.

  1. Fuel use: linear output and squared error

    In words

    The fuel head has no activation: its final sum is directly the prediction, 31.2 L/100 km. The truck used 33.0. We subtract, square, and also look at the other two regression losses.

    The math

    symbolvaluewhat it is
    31.2fuel use the network predicts (L/100 km)
    33.0fuel use measured on the trip
    −1.8error: negative because the network fell short
    δ = 2Huber with a 2 L/100 km threshold: since the error is under 2, it uses the quadratic part, half the square

    And in liters and dollars?

    The trip was 180 km, so the diesel error is L. With diesel at $1.60/L (the price used throughout the collection), that is $5.18. The gradient −3.6 is negative: raising the prediction lowers the loss, and training will push it up.

    What it means: a small error gives a small penalty, 3.24 (L/100 km)². The units of the loss are those of the target squared: that will matter in step 4.

  2. Breakdown: sigmoid and binary cross-entropy

    In words

    The breakdown head ends in a logit . The sigmoid takes it to a probability. The truck did break down, so the penalty is −ln of that probability.

    The math

    Where do the numbers come from?

    is the base of natural logarithms, the ones PyTorch and scikit-learn use, so the loss is in nats. encodes “there was a breakdown”. The second form, , is what BCEWithLogitsLoss computes without going through . If there had been no breakdown, the penalty would be .

    What it means: the network gave 23% to something that happened: penalty 1.46. The push −0.77 raises the logit hard, three quarters of the largest possible.

  3. Trip type: softmax and cross-entropy

    In words

    Three logits, for urban, regional and highway. We exponentiate, divide by the sum and penalize with −ln of the probability “regional” got, which was the true type.

    The math

    Subtracting the maximum, as the stable code does

    Why does subtracting 1.6 change nothing?

    1.6 is the highest logit. Subtracting it divides the three exponentials and their sum by , and the factor cancels out when dividing. With these small logits it is not needed, but with logits of 800 the direct version would give nan (§2). is the one-hot of “regional”.

    What it means: the push raises the regional logit (−0.44) and lowers the other two in proportion to what they took (0.17 and 0.28). The three add up to zero: only the differences change.

  4. The total loss and who dominates it

    In words

    The network is trained with a single loss: the sum of the three. But each one is in its own units.

    The math

    Where does the 6 come from?

    6 L/100 km is, rounded, the standard deviation of fuel use over the 60 segments of topic 2 (6.07): how much fuel use varies from one trip to another. Dividing the error by it puts it in “standard deviations” and makes it comparable with the nats of the other two heads. If fuel use were measured in L/1,000 km, the MSE would be multiplied by 100 without the network being any worse.

    What it means: without standardizing, the fuel head makes up 61% of the loss with an error of only 1.8 liters; standardized, it drops to 4% and the breakdown, the error that is really large here, takes over.

  5. Confident and wrong

    In words

    Another, more confident network had given a breakdown logit of −4.6 and logits (3.4, −0.8, 0.6) for the type. We redo the math with what really happened.

    The math

    Why is there no ceiling?

    grows without bound as : each time the probability given to what happened is divided by 10, the penalty goes up by . The pushes, on the other hand, are bounded by 1: the network gets a strong but finite correction.

    What it means: the breakdown penalty is multiplied by 3.2 and the type penalty by 7.3. In a batch, examples like this dominate the mean; if they are labeling errors, they have to be cleaned.

  6. Dollars: the weight of a breakdown and the alert threshold

    In words

    A breakdown that slips through costs $4,000; a preventive inspection that was not needed, $300. With a class weight, each breakdown counts in the loss as many times as it costs more.

    The math

    Where do 4,000 and 300 come from?

    They are example figures for the fleet: the roadside breakdown adds up the tow truck, the urgent repair and the lost delivery; the inspection, the maintenance shop and half a day with the truck off the road. $926 is the expected cost of not alerting: the probability of a breakdown times what it costs. Since it is more than the $300 of the inspection, it pays to alert. With the 0.5 threshold the network would not have alerted.

    What it means: with a 23% risk, the unweighted network stays silent and the fleet pays $4,000. With weight 13.3 (or with the 7% threshold), the truck goes to the maintenance shop for $300. On 2,000 test trucks, that decision cuts the cost from $928,700 to $308,100 (§7).

ejemplo.py · reproduces the numbers above

"""Worked example: a 180 km trip through the three heads of the network, with each loss by hand."""
import numpy as np
from datos import VIAJE, SEGURO_Y_EQUIVOCADO, CLASES, COSTE_AVERIA, COSTE_REVISION
import perdidas as P

V = VIAJE
# 1) fuel use: linear output, squared error (and MAE and Huber to compare)
e = V["consumo_pred"] - V["consumo_real"]
print(f"1) error = {V['consumo_pred']} − {V['consumo_real']} = {e:.1f}   MSE = {e**2:.2f}   MAE = {abs(e):.2f}"
      f"   Huber(δ=2) = {0.5 * e**2:.2f}   ∂MSE/∂ŷ = {2 * e:.1f}")
litros = 180 * abs(e) / 100
print(f"   on the trip: 180 km × {abs(e):.1f}/100 = {litros:.2f} L  →  × $1.60/L = ${litros * 1.60:.2f}")
# 2) breakdown: sigmoid and binary cross-entropy
z = V["z_averia"]; p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
print(f"2) e^1.2 = {np.exp(1.2):.4f}   p = 1/(1 + e^1.2) = {p:.4f}   BCE = −ln p = {-np.log(p):.4f}"
      f"   (if there had been no breakdown: −ln(1 − p) = {-np.log(1 - p):.4f})   ∂/∂z = p − 1 = {p - 1:.4f}")
print(f"   with BCEWithLogits: softplus(1.2) = ln(1 + e^1.2) = {np.log1p(np.exp(1.2)):.4f}")
# 3) trip type: softmax and cross-entropy
zk = np.array(V["logits"]); ex = np.exp(zk); q = ex / ex.sum()
print(f"3) e^z = {ex.round(4)}   sum {ex.sum():.4f}   softmax = {q.round(4)}")
print(f"   CE = −ln {q[1]:.4f} = {-np.log(q[1]):.4f}   logsumexp = {np.log(ex.sum()):.4f} → {np.log(ex.sum()):.4f} − {zk[1]} = "
      f"{np.log(ex.sum()) - zk[1]:.4f}   ∂/∂z = p − y = {(q - np.eye(3)[1]).round(4)}")
print(f"   subtracting the maximum (1.6): e^(z − 1.6) = {np.exp(zk - 1.6).round(4)}, sum {np.exp(zk - 1.6).sum():.4f}")
# 4) the total loss of the three heads
L = [e**2, -np.log(p), -np.log(q[1])]
print(f"4) total = {L[0]:.2f} + {L[1]:.3f} + {L[2]:.3f} = {sum(L):.3f};  the fuel head contributes {L[0] / sum(L):.0%}")
Ls = [(e / 6)**2, L[1], L[2]]
print(f"   with fuel use standardized (÷ 6 L/100 km): {Ls[0]:.3f} + {L[1]:.3f} + {L[2]:.3f} = {sum(Ls):.3f}")
# 5) confident and wrong
S = SEGURO_Y_EQUIVOCADO
p2 = P.sigmoide(S["z_averia"]); q2 = P.softmax(S["logits"])
print(f"5) z = {S['z_averia']}: p = {p2:.4f} → BCE {-np.log(p2):.3f} ({-np.log(p2) / -np.log(p):.1f} times more);"
      f"  logits {S['logits']}: p(regional) = {q2[1]:.4f} → CE {-np.log(q2[1]):.3f};  pushes {p2 - 1:.3f} and {(q2 - np.eye(3)[1]).round(3)}")
# 6) class weights and the alert threshold
w = COSTE_AVERIA / COSTE_REVISION
print(f"6) w = {COSTE_AVERIA}/{COSTE_REVISION} = {w:.2f}   weighted BCE = {w * -np.log(p):.2f}   threshold 1/(1+w) = {1 / (1 + w):.4f}")
print(f"   p = {p:.4f} ≥ {1 / (1 + w):.4f} → alert; expected cost without an alert ${p * COSTE_AVERIA:.0f} vs inspection ${COSTE_REVISION}")

What would change in a real system

  • Batches, not one trip: the loss is the mean over thousands of trips, and each head may have labels for only part of them (not every trip has its “30 days later” resolved yet). The missing losses are masked.
  • Head weights chosen on validation, not by eye, and revisited if one task makes another worse.
  • Real costs: the $4,000 and $300 are examples; each fleet has its own and they change with the route and the load.
  • Calibration: with class weights, the probabilities are no longer frequencies; if you budget with them, recalibrate.
